Puyallup

The Puyallup Tribe’s own history connects its name and village histories with the Puyallup River mouth. A dated tribal-news report offers a second starting point through community efforts to create time and space for Lushootseed learning.

01

Identity and context

The Puyallup Tribe has homelands in the southern Puget Sound region.

Read the sources [1] puyalluptribe-nsn.gov

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Community-authored history, Lushootseed, treaty histories and contemporary government. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] puyalluptribe-nsn.gov [2] Puyallup Tribal Language Program — earlier linked resource [3] puyalluptribe-nsn.gov

03

Names and river villages

The Tribe explains its name through villages near the lower bend and mouth of the Puyallup River. Its account follows community life along rivers, prairies and saltwater before describing colonial settlement and treaty-era disruption. This is a tribal account of place and history, rather than a present-day boundary map or a substitute for the original treaty.

Read the sources [4] Puyallup Tribe of Indians

04

Making room for language practice

In her 2024 report, Molly Bryant describes the Language Program’s use of a dedicated immersion house. Amber Hayward and Zalmai Zahir explain why a setting separated from office interruptions can support everyday Lushootseed use. The account links conversation with ordinary shared activities; it is a dated report of teaching practice, not an independent measure of present fluency.

Read the sources [5] Puyallup Tribal News / Puyallup Tribe of Indians
